topicDisplay: Component 1 Drama Shakespeare And Other Drama
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The Aristotelian 'tragic hero' is conventionally a figure who is:
options: of high estate and essentially noble, whose downfall arises from error rather than mere vice
comic in temperament
entirely passive and faultless
wholly villainous and deserving of punishment
questions.explain: The classical tragic hero is elevated and largely virtuous, falling through hamartia rather than outright wickedness.

questions.q: 'Foregrounding' in stylistic analysis means:
options: placing a scene at the front of the play
making a linguistic feature prominent through deviation or repetition so it draws attention
summarising the plot's opening
describing the background setting
questions.explain: Foregrounding makes language conspicuous through patterning or deviation, directing the reader's interpretive attention.

questions.q: The 'soliloquy' is significant in Shakespearean tragedy because it:
options: grants the audience direct access to a character's private thoughts and moral struggle
allows the chorus to speak
provides the play's comic relief
resolves the plot mechanically
questions.explain: The soliloquy exposes a character's inner conflict, deepening tragic involvement and revealing motive.

questions.q: When two texts are compared, a 'point of divergence' is most valuable when it:
options: reveals how each writer handles a shared concern differently, illuminating both
shows the texts are completely unrelated
repeats a similarity already noted
proves one text is superior
questions.explain: Productive comparison uses difference to sharpen understanding of each text's distinctive method and meaning.

questions.q: In Doctor Faustus, the overreaching protagonist who barters his soul for forbidden knowledge illustrates the tragic convention of:
options: aspiration and transgression punished by an inexorable downfall
the comic resolution
the restoration of order through marriage
the faultless martyr
questions.explain: Faustus embodies tragic overreaching, his transgressive ambition driving an inescapable damnation.

questions.q: In tragedy, 'hubris' refers to:
options: the audience's pity
the hero's humility before the gods
excessive pride or overreaching that affronts the moral or divine order
the chorus's lament
questions.explain: Hubris is overweening pride or presumption that violates limits and invites the hero's downfall.

questions.q: The convention of the 'tragic waste' refers to:
options: the comic subplot's failure
the chorus's idleness
the destruction of much that is valuable, leaving a sense of loss beyond the hero alone
the absence of any deaths
questions.explain: Tragic waste names the loss of admirable lives and potential, deepening the catastrophe's emotional weight.

questions.q: An 'unreliable narrator' is one whose:
options: account the reader is invited to question because their credibility is compromised
narration is consistently omniscient and authoritative
perspective shifts between several characters
story is told entirely in the present tense
questions.explain: An unreliable narrator's version of events is undermined by gaps, bias or self-deception that the reader must read against.

questions.q: The 'tragic arc' of a conventional tragedy moves broadly:
options: in a circle returning to the start unchanged
from a position of stature, through error and reversal, to catastrophe and often recognition
from comedy to romance
from suffering to restored happiness
questions.explain: The tragic arc descends from elevation through hamartia and peripeteia to catastrophe, often by way of anagnorisis.

questions.q: In tragedy, a 'foil' character functions to:
options: narrate the play in verse
replace the chorus
resolve the plot mechanically
contrast with the hero so as to highlight the hero's qualities and choices
questions.explain: A foil sets off the protagonist by contrast, clarifying the hero's traits and the meaning of their decisions.

questions.q: The tragic emotion of 'pity' in Aristotle's scheme is typically aroused by:
options: the comic subplot
the hero's complete villainy
the restoration of order
undeserved misfortune befalling someone like ourselves
questions.explain: Pity, for Aristotle, responds to undeserved suffering, while fear arises from recognising the hero as like ourselves.

questions.q: Tragedy generally evokes a sense of 'inevitability' because:
options: the ending is happy
the hero faces no obstacles
cause and effect, character and fate combine so that the catastrophe feels both shocking and unavoidable
the plot is chosen at random
questions.explain: Tragic inevitability arises from the tight causal logic linking character, choice and fate toward the catastrophe.

questions.q: A response that explores how a text can sustain feminist, Marxist and psychoanalytic readings is primarily demonstrating which assessment objective?
options: AO3
AO4
AO5
AO2
questions.explain: AO5 rewards engagement with different interpretations, including the application of distinct critical lenses.

questions.q: In Tess of the d'Urbervilles, the protagonist's destruction by social judgement, chance and inflexible circumstance most closely fits the model of:
options: comic tragedy with a restorative ending
modern/social tragedy in which an essentially blameless figure is crushed by hostile forces
classical tragedy with a formal chorus
the wholly culpable tragic villain
questions.explain: Tess exemplifies a modern tragedy of victimhood, undone by social cruelty and circumstance more than personal fault.

questions.q: AO2 is best satisfied when a student:
options: lists the events of the plot in order
summarises three critics' opinions
describes the writer's life and times
analyses how specific choices of form, structure and language create meaning and effect
questions.explain: AO2 rewards close analysis of the writer's craft and the effects of formal, structural and linguistic choices.

questions.q: The 'connotation' of a word is:
options: its literal dictionary definition
the associations and overtones it carries beyond its literal sense
its number of syllables
its position in the sentence
questions.explain: Connotation refers to the implied associations a word evokes, as opposed to its denotative literal meaning.

questions.q: A 'new historicist' reading of a literary text would most characteristically:
options: focus only on the reader's emotional response
treat the text as one of many cultural documents circulating within and shaping the power relations of its period
read the text as a timeless expression of universal human nature
judge the text purely by its formal elegance and unity
questions.explain: New historicism situates a text among the period's other discourses, reading literature and history as mutually constitutive.

questions.q: In Aristotle's Poetics, 'hamartia' is best understood as:
options: the tragic hero's error of judgement or flaw that precipitates their downfall
the moment of fatal recognition
the audience's emotional purging at the play's close
the reversal of fortune from good to bad
questions.explain: Hamartia is the tragic hero's mistake or flaw, the error from which the catastrophe ultimately flows.

questions.q: 'Anagnorisis' is:
options: the inciting incident of the plot
the audience's catharsis
the moment of recognition when the hero grasps a crucial truth, often their own role in events
the chorus's opening ode
questions.explain: Anagnorisis is the tragic hero's moment of recognition, frequently coinciding with the reversal of fortune.

questions.q: A 'psychoanalytic' (Freudian) reading would typically attend to:
options: the rhythm and metre of the verse alone
the text's fidelity to historical fact
the unconscious, repression, desire and symbolic expressions of inner conflict
the economic base determining the cultural superstructure
questions.explain: Psychoanalytic criticism reads texts for unconscious drives, repression and symbolic enactments of psychic conflict.

questions.q: 'Framing' as a structural device most often refers to:
options: the use of iambic pentameter throughout
a story enclosed within another narrative that introduces and concludes it
the alphabetical ordering of chapters
the metaphors clustered in a single stanza
questions.explain: A frame narrative encloses an inner tale, often shaping how the reader judges its reliability and meaning.

questions.q: The 'inciting incident' in a tragedy is best described as:
options: the moment of recognition
the event that sets the tragic chain of cause and effect in motion
the final catastrophe
the audience's catharsis
questions.explain: The inciting incident triggers the causal sequence that drives the tragic action toward its catastrophe.

questions.q: In narrative theory, 'free indirect discourse' is best defined as:
options: direct speech reported within quotation marks
a first-person narrator addressing the reader directly
an authorial commentary that judges the characters explicitly
a character's thoughts rendered in the third person yet inflected with that character's own idiom and feeling
questions.explain: Free indirect discourse blends the narrator's third-person report with a character's voice, blurring the line between the two.

questions.q: At A-level, AO1 chiefly assesses a candidate's ability to:
options: analyse the influence of contexts on a text
articulate an informed, personal response using a coherent, accurate critical argument and terminology
analyse the writer's use of form, structure and language
explore how different readers interpret a text
questions.explain: AO1 rewards a coherent, well-written argument expressed in accurate critical terminology with relevant textual support.

questions.q: In a comparative essay, the strongest approach to comparison is to:
options: summarise text one fully, then text two, with no cross-reference
compare the authors' biographies in detail
note only that the texts share a theme
build an integrated argument in which texts are set against each other around shared concerns and differing methods
questions.explain: High-level comparison interweaves texts around a thesis, analysing similarities and differences in method and effect.

questions.q: Which AO is most directly engaged when a student discusses how a poem's original readers would have understood its references to colonial trade?
options: AO2
AO1
AO4
AO3
questions.explain: AO3 assesses understanding of the contexts in which texts are written and received.

questions.q: An 'ecocritical' reading would be most interested in:
options: the gendered power relations within the household
the text's depiction of class struggle
the relationship between the text, the non-human world and the environment
the repressed desires of the central characters
questions.explain: Ecocriticism examines how literature represents nature, place and humanity's relationship with the environment.

questions.q: Which is the best example of using context (AO3) analytically rather than as 'bolted-on' background?
options: Stating that the text was written in the nineteenth century
Listing the dates of the period at the essay's start
Showing how the poem's anxieties about industrialisation shape its imagery of the polluted river
A paragraph narrating the author's biography before discussing the text
questions.explain: Context is used well when it illuminates specific textual choices rather than sitting as detached background.

questions.q: The tragic structure of a Shakespearean play is often described as following a five-act movement; the 'climax' typically marks:
options: the comic interlude
the final couplet
the opening exposition
the turning point after which the hero's fortunes decisively decline
questions.explain: In the five-act model the climax is the pivot from which the hero's fortunes irreversibly fall toward catastrophe.

questions.q: A 'feminist' reading of a canonical play would most characteristically interrogate:
options: the rules of classical unity
the unconscious of the playwright alone
the iambic substitutions in the verse
how the text constructs, constrains or resists gender roles and female agency
questions.explain: Feminist criticism examines representations of gender, patriarchal structures and the agency afforded to women in the text.
